extractions.value: At presentation, she fulfilled clinical criteria for SPS (1, 2). She did not have Babinski signs. Supportive evidence for this diagnosis was the absence of lumbar lordosis in plain radiographs of the spine early in the course, the collapse of L4 and L2 vertebrae (thought to have been the result of lumbar paraspinal muscle spasms), and the presence of chronic inflammatory cells in the pancreas (some associated with islets) consistent with a reaction to anti-islet cell antibodies.

extractions.value: The patient developed new spells of paroxysmal leg jerking and apnea 2.5 years after onset of SPS. A spell was recorded with simultaneous video and polygraphic techniques. Autopsy showed diffuse encephalomyelitis characterized by perivascular cuffing in the spinal cord, brainstem, thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala and a dense mononuclear infiltrate in the anterior horns of the lumbar and cervical cord. The authors concluded the patient had an unusually long course of encephalomyelitis whose presenting clinical features resembled those of SPS.
extractions.quote: We conclude that, on balance, there is greater evidence to support the parsimonious hypothesis that this was a patient with an unusually long course of encephalomyelitis whose presenting clinical features resembled those of SPS.
